2	id: example.action-hierarchy.settings
3	type: example
4	title: Settings action hierarchy
5	summary: A settings screen separates routine profile actions from destructive account deletion.
6	tags:
7	  - action
8	  - destructive
9	  - settings
10	links:
11	  example-of:
12	    - pattern.action-hierarchy
13	  related:
14	    - component.button
15	assets:
16	  - id: light
17	    path: assets/action-hierarchy-settings.svg
18	    mediaType: image/svg+xml
19	    width: 960
20	    height: 640
21	    alt: Account settings screen with a secondary Cancel button and primary Save changes button in the profile form, followed by a separate danger zone containing a Delete account button.
22	annotations:
23	  - id: profile-actions
24	    label: Routine action group
25	    description: Cancel supports the task and Save changes completes it, so the group uses secondary and primary emphasis.
26	    references:
27	      - pattern.action-hierarchy#assign-emphasis
28	  - id: danger-zone
29	    label: Destructive action group
30	    description: Delete account acts on a different subject and is separated into a labeled danger zone.
31	    references:
32	      - pattern.action-hierarchy#separate-unrelated-decisions
33	  - id: outcome-labels
34	    label: Outcome-based labels
35	    description: Save changes and Delete account state their results without relying on color.
36	    references:
37	      - component.button#label-describes-result
38	---
39	
40	This account settings screen contains two independent action groups.
41	
42	The profile form pairs a secondary "Cancel" action with one primary "Save changes" action. The
43	primary action completes the routine editing task.
44	
45	Account deletion is destructive and operates on a different subject. A labeled danger zone
46	separates it from the profile form. Its supporting text explains the consequence before the person
47	reaches the destructive Button.
48	
49	![Account settings action hierarchy](assets/action-hierarchy-settings.svg)
50	
51	## What this example demonstrates
52	
53	- Hierarchy applies within an action group rather than across the whole page.
54	- A supporting action remains visible without competing with the primary path.
55	- A destructive action is separated from routine actions.
56	- Button labels name their results.
57	- Text and structure communicate purpose and risk without relying on color.
58	
59	## What this example does not decide
60	
61	The example does not define universal button ordering. Products must follow their established
62	reading direction and platform convention while preserving the semantic hierarchy.
63

1	---
2	id: pattern.action-hierarchy
3	type: pattern
4	title: Action hierarchy
5	summary: Assign action emphasis by importance, support role, and risk, and choose Button or Link by what the control does.
6	tags:
7	  - action
8	  - hierarchy
9	  - destructive
10	---
11	
12	Action hierarchy helps a person identify the next action without making every available action
13	equally prominent.
14	
15	## Define the action group
16	
17	An action group contains controls that resolve the same decision or task. A page can contain more
18	than one action group when the groups act on independent subjects.
19	
20	Use one `primary` Button for the highest-emphasis action in a group. Do not treat this as a rule that
21	allows only one primary action on an entire page.
22	
23	## Assign emphasis
24	
25	### Primary
26	
27	Use `primary` for the action that advances or completes the current task. Prefer one primary Button
28	per action group.
29	
30	### Secondary
31	
32	Use `secondary` for a supporting action that should remain visible. It can offer an alternative,
33	return to the prior state, or dismiss the current task without competing with the primary action.
34	
35	### Tertiary
36	
37	Use `tertiary` for a low-emphasis action that remains discoverable in context. Do not use it for the
38	main path through a task.
39	
40	### Destructive
41	
42	Use `destructive` only for a destructive or difficult-to-reverse action. It communicates risk
43	rather than hierarchy. In a destructive confirmation group, the destructive action can be the
44	highest-emphasis action and replaces the primary action.
45	
46	Do not use destructive styling for an error status, warning message, or action that merely needs
47	more attention. Status colors such as `danger` belong to Alert and Badge, not to actions.
48	
49	## Choose Button or Link
50	
51	Choose the control by what happens, not by how prominent it should look. A Button changes
52	something in the current view or submits a form. A Link takes the person somewhere: another page, a
53	location on this page, or a file. Do not style a Link as a Button to raise its emphasis, and do not
54	use a tertiary Button for navigation.
55	
56	A Link sits beside an action group, not inside its emphasis order. "View billing history" next to
57	"Save changes" is a Link because it leaves the task without resolving it.
58	
59	### Inline
60	
61	Use an `inline` Link inside a sentence. It inherits the surrounding type and stays underlined, so
62	it does not depend on color to be found.
63	
64	### Standalone
65	
66	Use a `standalone` Link on its own line or after the content it relates to, such as "View all
67	projects" under a list. It uses label type and shows the underline on hover.
68	
69	## Separate unrelated decisions
70	
71	Place destructive account or data management actions in their own labeled group. Do not mix a
72	destructive action into a routine save or cancel group when it operates on a different subject.
73	
74	## Use clear labels
75	
76	Name the result of each action. Labels such as "Save changes," "Discard draft," and "Delete account"
77	make the hierarchy understandable without relying on color.
78	
79	## Avoid
80	
81	- More than one primary Button in the same action group
82	- A primary and a destructive Button competing as terminal actions in one confirmation group
83	- Destructive styling used only to attract attention
84	- Tertiary styling for the action required to finish the task
85	- Disabled actions with no nearby explanation when the reason is unclear
86	- A Button that only navigates, or a Link that changes data or submits a form
87	- Relying on control order or color as the only expression of importance or risk
88

1	# @taproot-ds/web-components
2	
3	Framework-agnostic web components styled entirely with the design tokens from
4	[`@taproot-ds/tokens`](../tokens). No runtime dependencies and no bundler
5	required — just standard ES modules and custom elements.
6	
7	## Install
8	
9	```bash
10	pnpm add @taproot-ds/web-components @taproot-ds/tokens
11	```
12	
13	## Use
14	
15	Load the token stylesheet once, then import the components.
16	
17	```html
18	<link rel="stylesheet" href="/node_modules/@taproot-ds/tokens/dist/css/tokens.css" />
19	<script type="module">
20	  import "@taproot-ds/web-components";
21	</script>
22	
23	<ds-button variant="primary">Save changes</ds-button>
24	```
25	
26	The stylesheet is required: every colour, space and radius the button paints with
27	is a CSS custom property published by the tokens package. Because custom
28	properties are inherited, they cross the shadow boundary on their own. With no
29	`data-theme`, components follow the system color preference. Setting
30	`<html data-theme="light">` or `<html data-theme="dark">` overrides it.
31	
32	To register selectively, or under a different tag name:
33	
34	```js
35	import { defineButton } from "@taproot-ds/web-components/button";
36	
37	defineButton(); // <ds-button>
38	defineButton("acme-button"); // <acme-button>
39	```
40	
41	Every `src/<name>.js` is published as the subpath `…/<name>`, with types from
42	`src/<name>.d.ts`. Those types are written by hand. The package-root barrel,
43	`src/index.js` and `src/index.d.ts`, is generated by `build-index.js` during
44	`pnpm build` from the components in `src/` and is not committed. For JSX, map `ElementAttributes` (exported from the
45	package root) onto your framework's intrinsic elements. Helpers that are not public API belong in `src/internal/`,
46	which the `exports` map blocks. `…/index` is blocked too; import the package
47	root for the barrel.
48	
49	## Components
50	
51	Each component implements the technology-neutral contract in
52	`packages/spec/content/components/<name>/<name>.spec.yaml`.
53	`implementation/<name>.md` maps each web attribute, property, and event to the
54	spec's parameters and events, and holds web-specific guidance. Change it in the
55	same commit as the component's API. `pnpm spec get <name> --impl web` reads it.
56	
57	Every attribute has a matching property (`el.variant`,
58	`el.disabled`, …). Programmatic `focus()` and `blur()` forward to the inner
59	control. The host honors the native `hidden` attribute.
60	
61	## Editor and framework support
62	
63	The package ships a [custom elements manifest](https://github.com/webcomponents/custom-elements-manifest)
64	at `dist/custom-elements.json`, and `package.json` points to it with `customElements`. IDE plugins
65	and framework tools read it to offer each element's attributes, properties, events, slots, and CSS
66	parts. `pnpm build` writes it from the API tables in `implementation/` and the spec's descriptions,
67	so it matches `taproot get <name> --impl web`.
68	
69	## Forms
70	
71	`<form>` association does not cross shadow boundaries, so a naive web-component
72	control silently fails to submit. Form controls here are
73	[form-associated custom elements](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ElementInternals):
74	they use `ElementInternals` to find their form, contribute a value, report
75	validity, and follow an ancestor disabled `<fieldset>`. 
76	
77	```html
78	<form>
79	  <ds-text-field label="Email" name="email" type="email" required></ds-text-field>
80	  <ds-checkbox label="Send me the weekly digest" name="digest" checked></ds-checkbox>
81	  <ds-button type="submit">Subscribe</ds-button>
82	  <ds-button type="reset" variant="secondary">Clear</ds-button>
83	</form>
84	```
85	
86	## Styling escape hatch
87	
88	Each component exposes its inner surface as a CSS part named in its source:
89	
90	```css
91	ds-button::part(button) {
92	  letter-spacing: 0.02em;
93	}
94	```
95	
96	## Tokens consumed
97	
98	Every component consumes `--ds-semantic-*` tokens directly, plus primitives for
99	scale choices such as spacing and motion that have no semantic role. The tokens a
100	component reads are internal, not a customization API (tokens ADR 0003).
101	
102	## Styles are authored as real CSS
103	
104	Component styles live in `src/*.css` as ordinary stylesheets, so they can be
105	linted, formatted and reviewed with standard CSS tooling. `build-styles.js`
106	inlines each one into `dist/<name>.styles.js`, which the component imports and
107	adopts via `adoptedStyleSheets`:
108	
109	```
110	src/button.css   →   dist/button.styles.js   →   adopted into the shadow root
111	```
112	
113	The obvious alternative — `import sheet from "./button.css" with { type: "css" }`
114	— is the standards-track answer but is not shippable yet: Safari has no support,
115	Firefox 145 keeps it behind the `layout.css.module-scripts.enabled` pref, and
116	Vite needs a plugin. Inlining at build time keeps authoring in real CSS while the
117	published package stays plain ES modules that every bundler already understands.
118	
119	Run `pnpm run build` after changing a `.css` file, or `pnpm run watch` to rebuild
120	on save.
121	
122	## Tests
123	
124	Tests run in real Chromium through Vitest Browser Mode. From the repository root:
125	
126	```bash
127	pnpm exec turbo run test --filter=@taproot-ds/web-components
128	```
129	
130	Browser tests load the published token stylesheet (`test/setup/tokens.js`), so
131	every `var(--…)` resolves as it does on a page. `test/host-checks.test.js` runs
132	the shared host behavior (alias registration, `hidden`, parts, focus, events,
133	disabled handling, keyboard activation, `form`, enum properties, upgrade order)
134	against one row per component in `test/host-checks/<name>.js`; add a row file
135	when adding a component. Each
136	component also has its own `test/<name>.test.js` for behavior.
137	
138	`test/fixtures/gallery.js` holds one sample of every component; add one when
139	adding a component. `test/axe.test.js` checks each sample against WCAG A and AA
140	rules in both themes.
141	
142	### Screenshots
143	
144	CI compares each gallery sample, in both themes, against the Linux references in
145	`visual/__screenshots__`. Screenshots differ between operating systems, so this
146	is not part of `pnpm test`.
147	
148	When a change is intended, the CI run fails and its `visual-screenshots` artifact
149	holds the reference, actual, and diff images. After reviewing them, accept the
150	new screenshots and commit the result:
151	
152	```bash
153	pnpm --filter @taproot-ds/web-components exec node visual/accept-ci-screenshots.js
154	```
155	
156	To compare locally before pushing, create references for your own system from the
157	unchanged code, make the change, and compare. Those references aren't committed.
158	
159	```bash
160	pnpm --filter @taproot-ds/web-components test:visual --update
161	pnpm --filter @taproot-ds/web-components test:visual
162	```
163	
164	## Local development
165	
166	```bash
167	pnpm exec turbo run build --filter=@taproot-ds/web-components
168	pnpm exec turbo run test --filter=@taproot-ds/web-components
169	pnpm exec turbo run dev --filter=storybook --filter=@taproot-ds/web-components
170	```
171	
172	Turbo builds the token package before the component styles. `pnpm --filter`
173	runs this package's script only and will fail on a clean tree when `dist/` is missing.
174	
175	This package has no standalone demo. Each component's stories are in
176	`apps/storybook/stories/<name>.stories.js`. The `dev` task above runs Storybook
177	and rebuilds `dist/*.styles.js` whenever a `src/*.css` file changes.
178

2	component: component.text-field
3	package: "@taproot-ds/web-components"
4	tagName: ds-text-field
5	defineExport: defineTextField
6	usage: |
7	  <form>
8	    <ds-text-field label="Email" name="email" type="email" hint="Used for sign-in." required></ds-text-field>
9	    <ds-button type="submit">Continue</ds-button>
10	  </form>
11	api:
12	  - { name: label, kind: attribute, parameter: label }
13	  - { name: hint, kind: attribute, parameter: hint }
14	  - { name: error, kind: attribute, parameter: error }
15	  - { name: type, kind: attribute, parameter: type }
16	  - { name: name, kind: attribute, parameter: name }
17	  - { name: value, kind: attribute, parameter: value }
18	  - { name: placeholder, kind: attribute, parameter: placeholder }
19	  - { name: autocomplete, kind: attribute, parameter: autocomplete }
20	  - { name: disabled, kind: attribute, parameter: disabled }
21	  - { name: required, kind: attribute, parameter: required }
22	  - name: form
23	    kind: property
24	    type: "HTMLFormElement | null"
25	    description: The associated form, including association across the shadow boundary.
26	  - { name: input, kind: event, event: input }
27	  - { name: change, kind: event, event: change }
28	---
29	
30	## Forms
31	
32	Text field defaults to `type="text"`. Set `name` so the value is included when the form submits.
33	Pair it with Button to submit:
34	
35	```html
36	<form>
37	  <ds-text-field label="Email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required></ds-text-field>
38	  <ds-button type="submit">Continue</ds-button>
39	</form>
40	```
41	
42	A non-empty `error` marks the field invalid, associates that message with the control, and blocks
43	submit until the message is cleared. Use `hint` for guidance that is not an error.
44	
45	To validate in your own code, set `novalidate` on the form so the submit reaches your listener.
46	Read the values there, and set `error` on each field that needs a correction. Clear `error` on the
47	field's `input` event and when the form resets, because a reset leaves it set.
48	
49	The `value` attribute sets the initial value, which form reset restores. `autocomplete` takes the
50	HTML autofill tokens, such as `email` or `current-password`, so the browser can offer saved values.

2	component: component.alert
3	package: "@taproot-ds/web-components"
4	tagName: ds-alert
5	defineExport: defineAlert
6	usage: |
7	  <ds-alert variant="success" label="Changes saved" announce="polite" dismissible>
8	    Your profile is up to date.
9	  </ds-alert>
10	  <ds-alert variant="danger" label="Upload failed">
11	    <ds-icon slot="icon" label="Error"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10"/></svg></ds-icon>
12	    The file is larger than 10 MB.
13	    <ds-button slot="actions" variant="secondary" size="small">Choose another file</ds-button>
14	  </ds-alert>
15	api:
16	  - { name: variant, kind: attribute, parameter: variant }
17	  - { name: announce, kind: attribute, parameter: announce }
18	  - { name: dismiss, kind: event, event: dismiss }
19	parts:
20	  title:
21	    api:
22	      - { name: label, kind: attribute, parameter: label }
23	  dismiss:
24	    api:
25	      - { name: dismissible, kind: attribute, parameter: dismissible }
26	      - { name: dismiss-label, kind: attribute, parameter: dismissLabel }
27	      - { name: dismissLabel, kind: property, parameter: dismissLabel }
28	---
29	
30	## Slots
31	
32	The message uses the default slot. Put a `<ds-icon>` in `slot="icon"` and actions, usually
33	`<ds-button>` or `<ds-link>`, in `slot="actions"`. Empty icon and actions slots take no space. The
34	`label` attribute renders the title as text, not a heading. If the page outline needs a heading, put
35	one in the message.
36	
37	The live region for `announce` is inside the shadow root, around the title and message only
38	(`component.alert#announce-on-request`). The host never gains `role` or `aria-*` attributes.
39	
40	## The hidden attribute
41	
42	Dismissing sets the alert's own `hidden` attribute unless a `dismiss` listener calls
43	`preventDefault()` (`component.alert#dismiss-reports`). Setting `hidden` while the alert contains
44	focus moves focus on, however it was set (`component.alert#focus-after-dismiss`).
45	
46	## Framework notes
47	
48	- Render the alert, or remove `hidden`, when the event it reports happens. An announcing alert adds
49	  its text one frame after it connects or is unhidden, so a live region already in place announces
50	  it.
51	- Clear your state from the `dismiss` event, or the next render may still hold the hidden element.
52	- To send focus somewhere other than the next tabbable element, focus it from your `dismiss`
53	  listener.
